paragraphs: An important EU official has spoken about a factory in Ireland. The factory is called Aughinish Alumina. It is in Co Limerick.
The factory makes alumina. This is a white powder. It is used to make aluminium, a light metal.
David O'Sullivan works on EU sanctions against Russia. Sanctions are rules that punish a country. He said some of the factory's alumina helps the Russian army. He said there is "no doubt" about this.
A Russian company owns the factory. About half of its sales go to Russia. Several hundred people work there.
The EU is planning new sanctions against Russia. But the plan does not stop the factory's sales for now. The Irish Government says it will support any EU plan.
A senior EU official has said that material from a factory in Co Limerick is "undoubtedly" helping the Russian military. The factory, Aughinish Alumina, is near the village of Foynes.
David O'Sullivan is the EU's special envoy for sanctions. Sanctions are rules that limit trade with a country to put pressure on it. He spoke at an event in Dublin this week.

Aughinish makes alumina, a white powder used to produce aluminium. The plant is owned by Rusal, a large Russian metals company. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, its sales to Russia have grown a lot. Today they make up about half of its business.

In March, an investigation by The Irish Times and a group of reporters found that the alumina goes to Russian factories. The aluminium made there is later sold to companies that make weapons and missiles. Mr O'Sullivan said the reporters were right.

The European Commission is now preparing its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia. However, the draft does not include a ban on Aughinish's sales. Officials had thought about a limit on how much it could export, but they dropped the idea. They worry that a ban could cause problems for European companies that need aluminium.

The plant employs several hundred people and says it might have to close if the sales are banned. Estonia wants the EU to put sanctions on alumina. The Irish Government says it will support any measures the Commission proposes. All 27 EU countries must agree on new sanctions.
A senior EU official has said that alumina produced at a refinery in Co Limerick is "undoubtedly" supplying, at least in part, Russia's military industry.

David O'Sullivan, the EU's special envoy on sanctions and a former top official at the European Commission, made the comments at an event hosted by the Institute of International and European Affairs in Dublin. He said there was no doubt that investigative journalists had been correct about the plant's links with Russia.

Aughinish Alumina, near Foynes, is owned by the Russian metals giant Rusal. It produces alumina, a white powder that is the main raw material for aluminium. Its exports to Russia have risen sharply since the invasion of Ukraine and now account for around half of its business.

An investigation published in March by The Irish Times and the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project found that the alumina is shipped to Russian smelters. The metal is then sold to a Moscow trading firm that supplies alloys to arms and missile manufacturers.

Despite this, measures to stop the sales are not in the draft of the Commission's 22nd sanctions package. Officials privately considered a quota to gradually limit exports, giving the plant time to find new customers, but the idea has been shelved over fears of disrupting European supply chains. Mr O'Sullivan said any action must avoid harmful side effects.

The plant, which employs several hundred people, has warned that it could be forced to close if the shipments are banned. Estonia has proposed sanctions on alumina, and EU sources say a ban or quota has not been ruled out for later packages. Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said Ireland would support whatever the Commission proposes. Any new sanctions require the unanimous backing of all 27 member states.
